newsitem.title: KENYA: Mandela leaves "Great lakes" summit for home.
newsitem.headline: Mandela leaves "Great lakes" summit for home.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela discussed the conflicts in Zaire and Burundi with eight other African leaders for two hours on Monday before leaving the summit early and heading home.
Succumbing to international pressure to get involved, Mandela took part in high-level talks on the crisis in the "Great Lakes" region of Central Africa for the first time.
Zaire, the country at the heart of the conflict, stayed away from the summit in the Kenyan capital, dampening hopes for any breakthrough in the search for peace.
"It is hard to see what can be achieved without Zaire here," one delegate told Reuters.
Mandela took part in closed-door talks with other African leaders for a little over two hours before leaving to fly home.
Mandela apologised for the brevity of his stay.
He explained that South Africa's constitution barred both him and Vice-President Thabo Mbeki being abroad simultaneously.

"The whole question of the Great Lakes, particularly Zaire and Rwanda, has caught the attention of the entire world and it is absolutely necessary for us to exchange views confidentially and freely," Mandela said at the opening ceremony.
Zaire's absence, apparently in protest against what it says is Rwandan and Ugandan support for a major rebellion in the east, was a blow to hopes for progress.
Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi said in his opening speech it would have been "useful and helpful" if Zaire were present.
"The fact that Zaire is not here is regrettable but this must not deter us from deliberating on this problem," Moi said.

The summit, which was due to end by midday on Tuesday, was called to help the search for a ceasefire and political settlement in eastern Zaire and review policy on Burundi, where 150,000 Hutus and Tutsis have died in ethnic war since 1993.

Rebels in eastern Zaire launched a well-planned offensive in mid-October and now control key towns. They say their ultimate goal is to end the 31-year-old reign of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko who is due to return to Kinshasa on Tuesday after cancer surgery and convalescence in Europe.

The crisis in the Great Lakes -- an area roughly comprising Burundi, Rwanda and parts of Zaire, Tanzania and Uganda -- is potentially the most far-reaching in Africa since the Nigerian civil war in the late 1960s.
The French Foreign Ministry welcomed the Nairobi summit and hoped it would hasten the convening of an International Conference on the Great Lakes.
Zaire boycotted the first Nairobi summit on the Great Lakes on November 5, refusing to sit down with Rwanda which it accuses of sponsoring the rebellion.
Monday's boycott, despite what Moi said were assurances from Mobutu that Zaire would attend, confirmed that Kinshasa was still refusing to deal with Rwanda.
Mandela, on his first official visit to Kenya, joined the presidents of Eritrea, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe and Ethiopia's prime minister.
The rebels were not invited to take part, nor was Burundi's military regime, Kenyan officials said.
